title: FIGC in a Crisis as the Appointment of Pirlo Collapses
description: Paolo Maldini and Leonardo chose Andrea Pirlo as the next Italy coach after Pep Guardiola rejected it, but FIGC president Giovanni Malagò halted the procedures over some delicate off-the-pitch matter...
fullText:
Paolo Maldini and Leonardo chose Andrea Pirlo as the next Italy coach after Pep Guardiola rejected it, but FIGC president Giovanni Malagò halted the procedures over some delicate off-the-pitch matters, Corriere della Sera reports.

The young coach faced scrutiny for a contract with a Russian betting company, for which he serves as a global ambassador. Most European countries have cut ties at the start of the war in Ukraine. He clarified in a statement that there was nothing political behind it, but that didn’t stop the avalanche. The federal lawyer spent the weekend going over his contract, finding that it’s not directly tied to his role as manager of Dubai side United FC, which is owned by Sergey Lomakin, but rather a personal partnership.

That didn’t work in his favor, and Malagò canceled a meeting with Pirlo and his camp to go over the formalities.  The former midfielder ended his run with an Instagram post.

However, Maldini and Leonardo had threatened to resign over the former Milan midfielder not getting the job, seeing it as an attack on their supposed autonomy. The president will try to prevent it before assessing other candidates for the Azzurri. The duo believes the problem was strategically leaked because the choice wasn’t well-received due to technical reservations and the gaffer’s inexperience.

What a mess and an unforced error, as he shouldn’t have been hand-picked to begin with. They should have contemplated everything before throwing him into the fire. It’s easy to be in lockstep when the decisions are obvious; now it’s time for the officials to prove their caliber and character.

title: Real Madrid midfielder facing two months out after training injury
description: Real Madrid have been dealt a fresh injury blow just weeks before Jose Mourinho’s side get their 2026-27 season underway. The likes of Eder Militao and Rodrygo Goes are already confirmed to be absen...
fullText:
Real Madrid have been dealt a fresh injury blow just weeks before Jose Mourinho’s side get their 2026-27 season underway. The likes of Eder Militao and Rodrygo Goes are already confirmed to be absent for the start of the new campaign, and they have now been joined in the treatment room by young midfielder Thiago Pitarch.

Pre-season has been ongoing for the last two weeks at Valdebebas, although Mourinho has been without the vast majority of the players that were in international action over the summer. Pitarch was one of the few to have returned early after helping Spain win the U19 European Championship, as he sought to impress his new manager in order to be in his plans for the upcoming season.

Unfortunately, Pitarch’s hopes of impressing Mourinho have been curtailed by a knee injury, as per Diario AS. The teenager damaged the medial lateral ligament of his left knee during a recent training session, and he will now begin a spell on the sidelines.

According to the report, Pitarch will be out of action for 6-8 weeks. This means that he will not return to action until September, which is not only a big blow for himself, but also for Real Madrid, who had planned to seek an exit for the La Fabrica graduate.

Given that Mourinho prefers to count on Aurelien Tchouameni, Federico Valverde, Bernardo Silva and Eduardo Camavinga, and also the fact that Rodri could be signed from Manchester City, there was little chance for Pitarch to see regular action if he stayed at Real Madrid. In order not to affect his development, the plan has been for him to leave in search of regular minutes elsewhere, but interest could dry up now that he’s set for an extended spell on the sidelines.

title: Eric Garcia reflects on Spain World Cup win: ‘No coincidence that Ferran scored the World Cup winner’
description: Eric Garcia has revealed that his next major ambition is to win the UEFA Champions League with Barcelona after helping Spain lift the FIFA World Cup.The 25-year-old defender, one of eight Barcelona pl...
fullText:
Eric Garcia has revealed that his next major ambition is to win the UEFA Champions League with Barcelona after helping Spain lift the FIFA World Cup.

The 25-year-old defender, one of eight Barcelona players in Spain’s victorious squad, is currently enjoying a well-earned break before returning for the new season.

Speaking to COPE (h/t Mundo Deportivo), Garcia reflected on the World Cup triumph, praised teammate Ferran Torres and looked ahead to his objectives with Barcelona.

Garcia admitted he was deeply moved by the reception the squad received during the victory celebrations and reserved special praise for Ferran Torres, whose goal secured Spain’s World Cup title.

Asked about the sports psychologist he shares with the Barcelona forward, Garcia highlighted the mental work both players have put in throughout their careers.

Spain’s hero. (Photo by Buda Mendes/Getty Images)

“For better or for worse, and I can include myself in that, both Ferran and I are used to surprises. Our job is to play football, which I think is a privilege,” he said.

“Things, as I’ve always said, can go better, they can go worse, but you always have to be there, with the right attitude. And in the end, it’s no coincidence that he scored the goal that gave us the World Cup.”

Garcia also reflected on making his World Cup debut in the tournament’s biggest match, explaining that he had remained prepared throughout the competition despite not featuring earlier.

“I’d been preparing all month in case the opportunity arose, and look, it finally came in the final. And to win it, which was everyone’s goal. We were all there to contribute, whether we played or not,” the Barcelona defender said.

“I’d always told the manager I was ready for whatever came my way,” he added.

Champions League the next goal. (Photo by Alex Caparros/Getty Images)

The defender also revealed the moment Spain began to believe the trophy was within reach, saying:

“After Enzo’s sending-off and when they took Julian off and brought on another defender.”

Having added the World Cup to an already impressive list of honours, Garcia made it clear that his focus has now shifted to European success with Barcelona.

“Yes, yes. It’s clear that in the end I can’t complain about the record I have to this day. Every player wants to win, to win titles, and that’s what we’re here for,” he stated.

Garcia also confirmed that he is due to report back for Barcelona duty on 12 August as preparations continue for the new season.

title: Infantino tells critics to 'meditate, pray' as he hails World Cup
description: FIFA president Gianni Infantino has dismissed criticism on the governing body and the World Cup and accused opponents of "spreading hate and false rumours. " Infantino said in an lengthy Instagram post early Monday that the tournament in the United States, Mexico and Canada was "the most outstanding World Cup" which "celebrated humanity at its best.
fullText:
FIFA president Gianni Infantino has dismissed criticism on the governing body and the World Cup and accused opponents of "spreading hate and false rumours."

Infantino said in an lengthy Instagram post early Monday that the tournament in the United States, Mexico and Canada was "the most outstanding World Cup" which "celebrated humanity at its best."

He suggested that the critics “take a moment to reflect, meditate, pray, or watch a football match” because "our world needs love, not hate; tolerance, not division; celebration, not mourning."

Infantino highlighted the peaceful atmosphere at the 16 venues and that billions from around the world had watched the June 11-July 19 tournament.

"Sorry that the matches are now over and sorry that you missed all that joy and togetherness. Sorry that you were so consumed by hate and criticism that you missed it all," Infantino told the critics.

He said that while "you spread hatred we worked tirelessly to unite countries at war" and claimed that "Iran entered the United States without incident or conflict."

He did not mention criticism from the Iran team on the visa restrictions imposed on them by US authorities or the entry ban for designated Somali World Cup referee Omar Artan, rather highlighting that millions of others had no visa problems.

Infantino also dismissed criticism on refereeing and disciplinary matters which culminated in the lifting of an automatic red card ban for American player Folarin Balogun after an intervention from US President Donald Trump.

He said it was "curious" that the criticism came from countries where similar practices are "routine and widely accepted."

"Football is about unity, not division. Football is bigger than hate and discrimination," Infantino said in general terms, stating he was "incredibly proud" to have done his share.

title: Former Texas A&M DL cleared to return to Ravens after surgery
description: Former Aggie DL Nnamdi Madubuike, sidelined by a 2025 neck injury, has been cleared to return and begins 2026 on the Ravens’ PUP list.
fullText:
It has been a challenging year for former Texas A&M defensive lineman Nnamdi Madubuike, who went from one of the NFL’s premier interior disruptors to facing the possibility of never playing another down again.

After a breakout 2023 season and a new contract with the Baltimore Ravens, Madubuike followed up with a strong 2024 campaign, posting 6.5 sacks and 11 tackles for loss. Two games into the 2025 season, he already had two sacks and nine quarterback pressures, showing signs of returning to his dominant 2023 form until disaster struck. Following Baltimore’s Week 2 win over the Cleveland Browns, Madubuike began experiencing concerning symptoms in his neck and back.

The Ravens later confirmed a neck injury, sidelining him for the remainder of the season. Neck injuries are always unsettling, especially for defensive linemen, because the severity is often unclear and the risk of long‑term nerve damage increases dramatically in a sport built on violent contact.

Determined to get healthy and preserve his career, Madubuike underwent surgery in April. After months of rehab and consultations with specialists, an independent spine and cervical expert officially cleared him to return to football activities. With that encouraging news, the Ravens placed him on the PUP list entering the 2026 season.

The designation gives Madubuike the runway to ease back into the rhythm of an NFL offseason, rebuild strength, and gradually reintroduce contact under the supervision of Baltimore’s medical and performance staff. It’s a small but meaningful step toward seeing him back on the field at some point this season. A comeback that once felt far from guaranteed.

title: Days disrupted: Across the world, Iran war's effects trickle into everyday life one human at a time
description: The war in Iran began months ago and thousands of miles away.  Then the shock moved outward — into farms, factories and family budgets.  A severe shock to that system could push 45 million more people...
fullText:
HANOI, Vietnam (AP) — Across seven countries, seven people woke up to days that no longer looked the way they once did.

The war in Iran began months ago and thousands of miles away. But its effects quickly ricocheted across the world — oil markets first, sending fuel prices higher. Then the shock moved outward — into farms, factories and family budgets. Into the fabric of life.

The global economy remains tethered to fossil fuels that also drive climate change. A severe shock to that system could push 45 million more people into poverty, the United Nations Development Program warned.

For those far from the battlefield, the war arrived not as missiles or air raids, but through the disruptions of everyday life: businesses that no longer worked, goodbyes filled with fear, and livelihoods pushed closer to the edge.

Here are a few of their stories.

WHO/WHERE: Edgar Funelas, Manila

Funelas bathes beside his vehicle, moving quickly before the city wakes. He pours water over his head from a green pipe. Behind him, his jeepney stands still and worn. His 10-year-old daughter is asleep inside.

He uses laundry soap — harsher, but cheaper — to wash his body and his clothes in the same motion, stretching what little money he has. Even before the war in Iran, he was living on the margins. A fire took their home and their belongings, forcing them to move into the brightly colored minibus he drove.

He'd hoped to be able to rent a room by now. Then diesel prices surged and he could no longer afford the fuel to run his jeepney.

He hasn't earned a single peso in days. There will be no breakfast. Hunger gnaws, but it's the small rituals of privacy that he misses most: to be able to wash out of sight, to sleep behind walls, to keep his desperation from being laid bare.

That morning, after rinsing himself, he hopes to find work as a dispatcher at a nearby jeepney terminal — organizing the line of vehicles, calling drivers forward in turn, and packing passengers into each jeep.

For weeks, he and his daughter have been eating only what others can spare. She has already left school. At night, he drinks water and leaves the food for her, so she can go to bed with a full stomach.

Before the war, he made about $8 a day driving, sometimes twice that on good days. Now, for each vehicle he fills, he will earn about 16 cents — barely enough to buy a piece of bread.

"This is what we do. Coping and hoping prices will get lower. Hoping that the war will end. And to try to find ways to earn, so we can at least eat."

WHO/WHERE: Marlyn Garcia, New York

On a Tuesday morning, Garcia, 25, steps out of a food pantry with two bags filled with rice, pasta, fresh produce and other staples. The groceries will help feed her family through another week.

The food is free — a small reprieve for a household budget strained by higher gasoline prices after the war in Iran. But Garcia also has to calculate her days: doctor's appointments, her 3-year-old son's occupational therapy session, picking up her daughter, making dinner.

And before any of that, there is parking. Finding a street spot can take up to an hour. Each slow lap around the block burns fuel as the meter keeps ticking.

She came to New York from the Dominican Republic as a child and spent part of her teens in the city's shelter system with her mother. Today she works part time as a breastfeeding peer counselor in the Bronx. Her partner, Steven Espaillat, lost his job as a legal assistant in March and now picks up Uber shifts while searching for permanent work.

Their Toyota Camry has become indispensable. Three adults share it. Garcia and Espaillat use it the first half of the week; her mother-in-law uses it the second. That Monday, she bought gas at $3.97 a gallon ($1.05 per liter). With fuel prices in flux, every mile now has to be planned.

The family lives in a rent-stabilized apartment that costs $800 a month. Government food assistance helps fill the refrigerator. Higher gas prices are eroding their savings and she has begun taking every extra shift she can, especially those she can work from home.

Garcia still hopes to start graduate school, inspired by her son's developmental needs to help families like hers. She reminds herself that others have it worse. But the arithmetic of survival keeps getting harder.

Still, she keeps making the numbers work because of the two small children waiting at home. "It's summer so they always want an ice cream and I want to make sure I have that extra cash there for them," she says. "They shouldn't be able to suffer because of whatever is going on around the world."

WHO/WHERE: Oluwatosin Awodunmila, Lagos

Awodunmila and her husband, co-owners of a printing business in Somolu, a mixed-income residential suburb in central Lagos, arrive early as usual, after dropping their two children at school.

The street is silent, partly because the day is just beginning and partly because there was no electricity. The machines in the shops are off.

Awodunmila scans the shop and the leftover projects to make — lip gloss, key holders, paper bags. But she has to wait for electricity, which hardly comes nowadays. The other option is to fire up the medium-sized generator outside the shop. But since the war began, the price of fuel per liter has nearly doubled from 800 naira to 1,400 naira (60 cents to $1).

This jump in price has brought business to almost a halt. In Nigeria, the retail price of fuel determines the price of everything else. If they use the generator, the profit margin thins to almost nothing. They had decided not to increase the price of their service to keep their customers.

So they wait for electricity and sit, like on this morning, while customers lodge complaints about slow delivery. On Monday, four days earlier, there was no electricity until 7 p.m., and the fuel consumption for that day alone was 30,000 naira ($21.85), more than half of what they had hoped to earn on the day's jobs.

Recently, they changed their delivery policy from one business day to three to five working days.

"My biggest wish right now is a 24-hour supply of electricity and the war in Iran to end — and, of course, the cost of fuel should come down."

WHO/WHERE: 54-year-old mother, Kathmandu

The house is quiet again. She checks her phone, hoping her son has landed. It is still too early to expect a reply. Somewhere between Nepal and Abu Dhabi, he is returning to the hotel where he works after a visit home.

She asked not to be identified, fearing her son could face repercussions at work.

The war in Iran has made this goodbye harder. Images of missiles and airstrikes, and reports of migrant workers killed in the conflict, have left her agonized. She reaches for her phone again.

That morning, the house was full. Friends and relatives gathered to see her son off. She moved between the kitchen and the prayer room, serving tea and praying for his safe journey. Incense, conversation and the ringing of a prayer bell filled the house. The dog barked, unaware a farewell was underway.

They drove to Kathmandu's international airport, where departures are measured as much in embraces as boarding passes. She hugged her son tightly before he joined a queue of young men bound for the Gulf, whose remittances account for about 10% of Nepal's GDP.

She stood there until he disappeared from view, tears streaming down her face.

The 54-year-old is a cleaner at a bank, but her son's income is essential. Her husband, who owned a small soap factory, died of COVID in 2021, leaving much of the family's financial burden to their children. Her daughter works for a finance company in Kathmandu but, like her brother, hopes to build a future overseas.

As the United States and Iran negotiate a permanent end to the war, there is little the mother can do but wait. She keeps her phone close, hoping it will ring and confirm her son is safe.

"I am wondering how he is going to live. We can't just say, don't go. But at the same time, it is necessary that he goes."

WHO/WHERE: Felipe Molina, Santiago

Molina clicks his seat belt into place, shifts his yellow-roof taxi into gear and eases into Santiago's evening traffic.

In the rearview mirror, the 50-year-old wears the look of someone trying to solve an impossible equation. He can keep driving, burning diesel in search of passengers, or pull over and hope they find him. Either way, he loses.

The Peruvian has lived in Chile for more than 25 years and spent 17 behind the wheel of one of the city's traditional taxis. Over that time, he has weathered traffic jams, recessions and the pandemic. But soaring fuel prices since the war in Iran have turned every shift into an effort to lose less.

He drives passengers. He delivers packages. On the radio, a commentator's voice rises as Spain takes on Belgium in the World Cup. At a red light, a street performer in clown makeup waves burning flares between rows of idling cars. Molina inches forward, piecing together enough fares to keep his taxi on the road.

In March, Chile's government announced one of the country's largest fuel price increases in recent years as global oil prices climbed. Molina now spends about 70% more to fill his tank.

The higher fuel costs have compounded existing pressures. Ride-hailing services such as Uber and the Chinese company Didi are luring away passengers with lower fares. Meanwhile, licensed taxi drivers cannot raise prices because fares are regulated by the government.

Chile responded with monthly subsidies for taxi drivers and other public transport drivers, froze public transport fares and expanded programs to help drivers replace older vehicles.

But for Molina, the support hasn't changed the equation.

"In the end, we spend hours on the road without picking anyone up, and the fuel keeps running out," he says. "That means I have to fill up again, and the cost is simply too high."

WHO/WHERE: Ali Osman Aykul, Istanbul

Most days, Ali Osman Aykul has only his cat for company.

The grey cat, Prince, sleeps on a stack of hand-woven carpets while Aykul, 48, smokes cigarettes, sips tea and watches football. Richly colored Turkish carpets line the walls. Their intricate patterns radiate warmth. Occasionally, footsteps drift in from the bazaar outside, but most pass by.

Before the war in Iran, the shop was where wealthy collectors from around the world and especially the Gulf gathered. Then the fighting began. Within 10 days, business fell by 90%. Airports closed; international customers vanished. Now, a handful might wander in each day — but mostly to buy cheap souvenirs, not the handmade carpets.

The bills have not stopped. Electricity, rent and his daughter's school expenses — she is studying healthcare — still need to be paid. To cope, Aykul doesn't buy new clothes, cooks his meals in the shop and listens to music there rather than going out.

He holds out his newly issued passport with hope, tempered by doubts about whether, even if the war ends, trade will return to what it was. Before the pandemic, he traveled regularly to international fairs, where collectors sought him out. Now he waits for his visa, hoping that if customers can no longer come to his carpets, he can go to them.

"After a while, it starts to weigh on you every day," he says. "The music you listen to begins to feel like torture, and even the tea you drink stops giving you any pleasure."

WHO/WHERE: Enzo Garbaglia, Fiumicino (Rome)

His blue tractor still needs fuel. What has changed is how Enzo Garbaglia buys it.

For years, the farmer outside Rome bought gasoline in bulk, bringing home 1,500 to 2,000 liters (400–530 gallons) at a time and storing it for the season ahead. Now he buys only enough to keep the tractor moving.

Fuel is only the beginning. Irrigation costs more. Fertilizer costs more.

Garbaglia tries to shield customers, but many are struggling too. They buy less, produce goes unsold and prices fall. By the time he brings his harvest to market, a day's work yields little profit, if any.

Across the 105-year-old family farm, there are other signs of sacrifice and strain. The machines Garbaglia uses to harvest potatoes are the same ones he has relied on for years. There is no money to replace them. At home, the family avoids unnecessary expenses. Even a few weeks off in the summer to recover from long days in the fields is a luxury.

His children do not plan to take over the farm. For a time, his daughters seemed poised to continue the family tradition. Their farm-to-table shop drew customers from Rome and the surrounding coast. But after years of struggle, they concluded farming no longer offered a future and walked away. The decision hurt but he was also relieved they had chosen a different path.

Now, Garbaglia is left tending the land his family has worked for over a century, driven by passion for farming, loyalty to customers and pride in offering quality.

But he knows what comes next. The family business will likely end with him.

"One hundred and five years of history can't be sold," he says. "When it ends, it ends. That's it."

title: Explainer-How Singapore's unique monetary policy works
description: SINGAPORE, July 27 (Reuters) - Singapore's central bank tightened its monetary policy settings unexpectedly on Monday, with inflation projected to step up in the months ahead. Singapore's central bank has a unique ‌method of managing monetary policy, tweaking the exchange rate of its currency instead of changing domestic interest ‌rates like many economies.
fullText:
SINGAPORE, July 27 (Reuters) - Singapore's central bank tightened its monetary policy settings unexpectedly on Monday, with inflation projected to step up in the months ahead.

Singapore's central bank has a unique ‌method of managing monetary policy, tweaking the exchange rate of its currency instead of changing domestic interest ‌rates like many economies.

The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) sets the path of what it calls the policy band of the Singapore dollar nominal ​effective exchange rate (S$NEER), thus strengthening or weakening the local currency against those of its main trading partners.

WHY DOES SINGAPORE USE THIS METHOD?

Singapore is a small and trade-reliant economy. Gross exports and imports of goods and services are more than three times its gross domestic product (GDP). Almost 40 cents of every Singapore dollar spent domestically is on imports.

That means the exchange ‌rate has a much bigger influence ⁠on inflation than domestic interest rates.

For example, an appreciation of the Singapore dollar against the currencies of its major trading partners will reduce prices of imported goods and services. This ⁠dampens the prices that households have to pay.

The S$NEER is an index of the Singapore dollar's trade-weighted exchange rate against the currencies of the island's major trading partners.

The central bank says this allows the Singapore dollar to perform ​collectively in ​relation to its major trading partners, which is what matters ​for general price levels in Singapore.

HOW DOES THE ‌S$NEER POLICY BAND WORK?

MAS does not set the precise level of the exchange rate or control it in real time. Instead, the S$NEER is allowed to move up and down within a policy band, the exact levels of which are not disclosed. If it goes out of this band, the MAS steps in by buying or selling Singapore dollars.

The policy band has three parameters that the MAS can adjust. Until 2024, these parameters were reviewed at ‌least twice a year, typically in April and October.

Additional reviews can ​be held if conditions demand an immediate change in settings, such ​as in 2022 when high inflation triggered two ​off-cycle moves.

From 2024, the central bank started making monetary policy announcements every quarter, saying it ‌allowed policymakers to provide their assessment of the ​economic outlook in a more ​timely fashion.

The three policy levers are the slope, the level and the width of the band.

Adjusting the slope will influence the pace at which the Singapore dollar strengthens or weakens.

description: The United States and Iran paused their attacks for a second straight day Sunday, as efforts continued to bring them back to negotiations on an interim ceasefire deal largely undermined by recent exch...
fullText:
CAIRO (AP) — The United States and Iran paused their attacks for a second straight day Sunday, as efforts continued to bring them back to negotiations on an interim ceasefire deal largely undermined by recent exchanges of fire.

It was not clear why the U.S. has paused after targeting Iranian coastal areas and infrastructure in a nearly two-week escalation sparked by Iran's firing at ships trying to transit the Strait of Hormuz. The Pentagon did not respond to questions.

U.S. President Donald Trump is "giving talks some space. He's giving it a little bit of room," Mike Waltz, the U.S. ambassador to the United Nations, told Fox News. "We've had both Oman and Iran, and a number of our other negotiators, engaged at every level, from the most senior levels all the way down to the technical level over the past few weeks, and particularly in the past few days."

Waltz dismissed the idea that the U.S. stockpile of interceptors crucial in defending against Iranian attacks is running low, but experts have questioned how long both the U.S. and Iran can afford to keep up attacks.

Since the U.S. has halted attacks for the past two nights, Iran has as well, its army spokesperson told Iran's state TV on Sunday. Tehran in recent days has counterattacked against countries in the region hosting U.S. military forces, killing at least three service members at a base in Jordan and one in Iraq.

The 60-day period that began when the interim deal was signed by both countries in mid-June is now well into its second half, and major issues that were meant to be negotiated -– notably Iran's nuclear program at the heart of tensions -– remain set aside as mediators try to keep both sides talking.

A regional official involved in mediation efforts said diplomacy was underway and that a pause in U.S. and Iranian strikes was a "positive signal that helps their efforts to de-escalate."

The official said both countries want to return to the interim ceasefire deal and that a compromise being negotiated centers on having Iran run vessel transit through the Strait of Hormuz with fewer restrictions on ships. The official was not authorized to discuss the matter and spoke on condition of anonymity.

Concerns continued about shipping on the strait and now on another crucial waterway in the region, the Bab al-Mandeb strait to the Red Sea. Iranian-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen last week threatened a blockade of Saudi shipping there.

Global energy supplies and the economy remain in the balance as gasoline prices have risen again.

Commercial shipping traffic on the Strait of Hormuz was at a three-week low, a maritime body overseen by the U.S. Navy said Sunday, adding that no new attacks had been confirmed in the past 72 hours. It said traffic remained steady through the Bab el-Mandeb.

Iran on Sunday said it continued to speak with Oman about managing the safe passage of ships on the Strait of Hormuz, which passes between the countries. Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesperson, Esmail Baghaei, said talks had made progress and continued.

Baghaei also said the strait's status remained unchanged. Tehran has asserted that the interim deal with the U.S. allows it to manage shipping on the waterway for now, and it has objected to U.S. efforts to support a route through the strait that passes close to Oman instead. The strait was considered an international waterway before the war.

The U.S. military on Saturday said its recently reimposed naval blockade against Iran continued, with a dozen commercial ships redirected, two disabled and two boarded. U.S. forces "remain highly vigilant, focused, lethal, and ready," it added.

Meanwhile, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu plans to travel to the United States and meet with Trump in Washington on Tuesday, his office has said. They last met in Washington in February, weeks before they launched the war on Iran that killed senior leaders including Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.

The Iranian-backed Hezbollah fired at Israel two days after the war began, and Israel responded with airstrikes and ground forces in southern Lebanon. Since then, the U.S. has supported landmark direct talks between Lebanon and Israel to try to calm that front and find a way to disarm Hezbollah.

Netanyahu on Sunday told Fox News he "fully" backs Trump's efforts to weaken Iran and press it to end its nuclear program, adding: "If he can do so without returning to intense military fighting, that's fine. Why not?"

The prime minister indicated he would not present new information to "our good friend" Trump and instead would listen to "what he has in mind, because I think in many ways, it's his decision."

But Netanyahu warned that if Iran again attacks Israel, directly or with armed proxies, "it will make a terrible mistake."

Anna reported from Lowville, New York. Associated Press writers Darlene Superville and Ben Finley in Washington contributed.

fullText:
The horror movie sensation of 2026 has its roots in gaming’s discovery of ‘noclip’ – and the hidden virtual realms that could be opened up inside games. Developers explain how everyone got lost in these liminal spaces

It starts on 4chan, in a May 2019 thread entitled “unsettling images”. The first post was a photo showing an empty room with the now iconic yellow wallpaper, no natural lighting and a kind of inexplicable jutting half-wall. Shortly afterwards, another user (there are no usernames on 4chan, just identifying numbers) responded with 78 words of text that would essentially lay out the blueprint for a future $262m A24 movie sensation.

“If you’re not careful and you noclip out of reality in the wrong areas, you’ll end up in the Backrooms,” the post begins. For the uninitiated, “noclip” refers to a game mode in which collision with solid objects is disabled, allowing players to move freely through walls and floors. Think of Chiwetel Ejiofor’s character in the film, finding a permeable wall in the basement of his furniture store and passing through to the world on the other side.

In games, noclip is intended for use by developers testing out their creations – but for decades now, players have been finding ways to access it themselves and reach hidden places they were never intended to see. It’s a phenomenon that Studio Chyr creative director William Chyr is intimately familiar with, both as a maker of games and as a player.

“Going behind the scenes, noclipping, and seeing the logic of the space, it’s like this Wizard of Oz moment of pulling open the curtain,” Chyr says. He remembers an early encounter with this in Batman: Arkham City: “There was this glitch that allowed you, if you kept spamming one of the grenades, to keep going higher and higher.” From there, the caped crusader could soar outside the level, into sections of Gotham that were only ever intended as a backdrop. “The streets had these cars that moved, but it was just a flat texture.”

Watching Backrooms, Chyr was also reminded of a similar bug in the notoriously janky Skyrim, where holding a wooden plate provided a quick way of noclipping out of the world. Looking at it from the outside in, players discovered that many of the game’s “tables” were in fact just bookcases embedded deep in the ground – just like the memorable Backrooms shot of a room in which the furniture is clipping through the floor. All these things that, in video games, the player is never meant to see.

The feel of Kane Parsons’ film is actually closer to these experiences than any of the many “official” Backrooms games that have popped up. The open-source nature of this mythos (as well as 4chan and Reddit, there are sprawling fan wikis cataloguing and expanding the lore) means that it’s possible to release your own game set in the Backrooms, using the name and iconography, in a way you couldn’t with another horror movie.

The most high-profile of these games, Escape the Backrooms, was first available in early-access form in August 2022, just months after Parsons’ first video. It offers a perfectly faithful recreation of the Backrooms aesthetic, from the yellow hallways to the yellow hazmat suits worn by agents of Async, the mysterious organisation only introduced towards the end of the film but a mainstay of the online incarnations. But all this is just wallpaper applied over the blueprint of a multiplayer survival horror game.

At its best, Backrooms taps into a sense of a place being “off”, in a way that’s unsettling but hard to pin down. It’s a delicate sensation, easily shattered (as it is in the film, I’d argue) by the presence of killer monsters. Even more so by the sight of another player in their gas mask and reindeer onesie, bunny-hopping through the hallways ahead.

Thankfully, there’s another stripe of Backrooms-inspired games offering nothing more than a self-guided tour through environments with a growing sense of weirdness and the constant suggestion of a threat lurking out of view.

Pools and Dreamcore both shine a spotlight on Poolrooms, an infinite swimming-baths dimension first glimpsed in one of Parsons’s videos and codified by the fandom as Level 37 of the Backrooms, with a similarly alien approach to architecture. In Dreamcore, it’s just one of a selection pack of realms to explore. You’ll also explore a “dead mall” and the looping corridors of a hotel: both abandoned and seemingly endless, like the spaces explored in the film, but with less of an obvious supernatural edge.

These malls and hotels are prime examples of a larger online taste for liminal spaces from which Backrooms is just one offshoot.

“These spaces always feel like they’re past their prime,” says Chyr. “It’s clear there was human activity here, at one point, but no longer.” His 2025 game Hotel Infinity is steeped in all these ideas, to the extent that at one point Hotel Liminal was considered as a title, Chyr says. “But I thought that was just too on the nose!”

Set in the lifeless corridors of a hotel seemingly designed by MC Escher, it’s a VR game that uses some clever spatial trickery to fold its endless halls into a 2x2m square of your living-room floor. One particular sequence late in Backrooms made me think of Chyr’s game – he confirms that he thought the same thing. “I was like, damn, I wish we’d done that!” he laughs.

Hotel Infinity is primarily focused on the impossible architecture of these places, something it shares with Exit 8 (also adapted into a film this year), a Japanese-made game that traps you in an infinitely looping section of a Tokyo metro station. The other side of the liminal coin is the sensation summoned by that original 4chan image: the eeriness of an empty place that no longer has any obvious function, or perhaps never did.

One game exploring this aspect is Interior Worlds, a “liminal photography” game in which you explore such spaces armed only with an SLR camera. The game’s developer, who goes by the moniker Sodaraptor, remembers first encountering the concept of liminal spaces “back in 2020, when the original Backrooms post on 4chan started going viral.”

It was an emotion they’d felt in such places but never previously had a name for. “A strange liminal discomfort”, Sodaraptor says, mixed with pangs of “anemoia”: nostalgia for an era that predates your own experience.

So it’s only fitting that the phenomenon’s virtual inspirations are now, in video game terms, as ancient as all those dead malls.

The aforementioned Arkham City and Skyrim both came out in 2011. The same year, Valve released Portal 2, the mind-bending first-person puzzler which Parsons has repeatedly cited as his biggest influence. The director even made a couple of Portal fan-videos; the last one was uploaded to his YouTube channel in 2021, just months before the first Backrooms clip.

It is probably inevitable that the aesthetics of these 15-year-old games would just now be beginning to seep through into the cinematic mainstream. Parsons was a young child when Portal 2 came out, and it’s only natural that he – and the generation of film-makers just now coming of age – would make things informed by the dark rooms they got lost in as kids.

A Minecraft Movie may already exist (unfortunately) but what will be much more interesting are the films and other artworks shaped by the experience of playing Minecraft at a formative age. Those dark caverns, the endless mines, the sounds of the zombies, the threat of the creepers – once those strange experiences have sunk into internet lore, who knows what will emerge and where it will take us.

title: For a few seconds, AusAlert blared around parks, libraries and cinemas – but some didn’t get the alert at all
description: Federal government touts emergency warning alert test as a success and says no approach works 100% of the...
fullText:
Federal government touts emergency warning alert test as a success and says no approach works 100% of the time

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

A blaring emergency warning alert Australians had been warned about was anti-climactic for some – and totally missed by others.

Almost every phone in the country, alongside some smartwatches and tablets, was supposed to let off a loud noise at about 2pm AEST and receive a pop-up notification with the text “TEST MESSAGE” and “NO ACTION IS REQUIRED”.

The event was the first nationwide test of a new warning system called AusAlert, which will be deployed in October to prepare Australians for fires, floods, terrorist incidents or health emergencies.

The federal government has spent the past week telling the public about this test alert.

But for many, it came and went in just a few seconds.

Indigo Miller was working from home in Canberra when her colleagues reminded her of the notification.

“I was counting down for two minutes before,” she says.

“But it was pretty anti-climactic and I think I accidentally clicked it away.

“Mine also wasn’t super loud so if I was outside and my phone was inside, I don’t know if I would hear.”

Miller had attempted to film herself recording to try capture the sound of the alert, but her phone cut out as the siren went off.

Busker Dani Bainbridge was about to start performing at Sydney’s Hyde Park when the alert began pinging.

“It did the job, I think,” she said.

But others did not receive an alert at all.

Guardian Australia received reports of mobile users whose phones got a notification but did not blast a sound.

Prior to the test, the National Emergency Management Agency received advice about 80% of Apple iPhones would ring, as well as 16m Android devices.

It also said the alert would go to iPhone models 11 and up running iOS 26.4 or later, Apple Watch models SE2, SE3, Series 6 and up running watchOS 26.4 or later, and Android devices running Android 12 or later.

Guardian Australia was told of an iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 17 Pro, iPhone 12, a Samsung phone and other devices not receiving a notification despite being on.

The federal emergency management minister, Kristy McBain, said 94% of targeted cell towers had successfully broadcast the alert.

“Don’t worry if you did not receive an alert – this could be because you were not in a coverage area, your software was not up to date or your device was incompatible,” she said.

“Nema will continue to analyse the technical and performance data and engage with emergency service organisations around the country.”

Asked if it would ever be completely successful, McBain said “there is no one avenue of communication that is 100% successful”.

“This technology is more reliable than the current text-based technology,” she said.

“But as I said, this is just another tool in the toolkit for emergency service agencies, who are doing a really good job in communicating to communities that are at risk during a natural disaster.”

Ahead of the AusAlert test, domestic and family violence advocates raised concerns about the risk of the notification exposing “safe phones” and urged people to keep devices hidden for safety reasons.

AusAlert interim coordinator general Pat Hetherington said the advice for people who have safe phones and hidden phones is for them to be switched off for a 24-hour period.

Businesses and people going about their daily lives reacted to the impending alert in different ways.

Before the alert, those who had bought Imax tickets for Christopher Nolan’s much-anticipated The Odyssey at the 1.50pm session in Sydney were told by workers to switch off their phones.

Though some still went off, they rang out during the ads that played before the film, according to people present in the theatre.

At the State Library of NSW, the siren cut through the typical wall of silence, offering some reprieve to cramming Year 12 students and even waking up one high schooler who was nodding off at his laptop.

fullText:
Research shows AI accounts are gaining millions of views on TikTok by spreading dubious health advice

Misleading health claims online pose a “huge danger to public safety”, experts have warned, after research has shown that AI-generated doctors are gaining millions of views on TikTok by spreading dubious health advice.

The British Medical Association council deputy chair, Dr Emma Runswick, flagged the risks posed by AI accounts that “peddle medical myths and promote so-called miracle cures”.

“Platforms like TikTok must do more to stop the rise of dangerous fake medical advice … otherwise, it is the public who could be paying the price with their health and perhaps even their lives,” she added.

AI-generated physicians were found to have spread disproven myths about cancer, including that microwaving food in plastic, using deodorants and sleeping next to your phone could all cause cancer – all claims which have been refuted by Cancer Research UK.

The research was published this month by Hallam, a digital marketing agency. It follows warnings by the NHS that health misinformation on social media was a “real threat to public health”.

The research found that AI-generated content appeared in 40% of top health-related TikTok videos, with most posted by a growing number of deepfake influencer accounts designed to resemble real doctors. For some specific search terms, such as “health tips”, 84% of videos were classed as AI-generated or AI-assisted content.

According to Hallam, top AI-generated doctor and health videos in their search received an average of 2.5m views. TikTok took down examples of the videos that were sent to the platform by the Guardian.

The accounts also promoted bizarre remedies for various health problems, including Coca-Cola mixed with onion as a pain-relief remedy and a fake product called “Hyalethinap Plus Pro Max” as an anti-ageing solution.

One avatar claimed he had recommended “Hyalethinap Plus Pro Max” to his patients for years, and that it could combat “hair loss, skin weakening, brittle nails and joint pain” by helping the body produce “anti-ageing molecules naturally”. The Guardian could not find evidence of “Hyalethinap Plus Pro Max” products online.

In response to the findings, Prof Frankie Swords, the national medical director at NHS England, said it was concerning to see a rise in online medical misinformation. “Many clinicians are reporting an increasing number of patients who feel worried and confused due to false advice that has been made solely for clicks,” she added.

Prof Victoria Tzortziou Brown, the president of the Royal College of GPs, said she was also concerned by the research, adding that misleading AI content carried a “real risk” of harm.

Hallam analysed 1,198 videos, selecting the top 50 videos across a series of search terms including “health tips” and “doctor advice”. It also looked for general “life-impacting” advice on issues such as personal finance and education.

Alex Ruani, health misinformation researcher at UCL, said the rise of AI doctor videos represented a “frightening amount of exposure to fake medical content”.

“We’re looking at industrialised exploitation of trust,” she added.

Last year, a poll conducted by Savanta on 3,575 men and 3,832 women aged 18 and above in England on behalf of patient champion Healthwatch England found that about one in five people were using social media for health information.

William Pett, interim director of policy and public affairs at Healthwatch England, said: “Without the skills to distinguish reliable information from commercial hype or misinformation, [people] risk being misled in ways that can seriously affect their health.”

A TikTok spokesperson said: “These findings from a marketing agency with commercial interests are not an accurate reflection of our platform.”

“The facts are that we remove harmful health misinformation, including when it’s AI-generated, we partner with the World Health Organization and the NHS on providing reliable health information in-app, and we continually invest in AI literacy resources and labelling technologies.”

title: I risk losing my livelihood because Nissan failed to repair my car

fullText:
I’m a self-employed driving instructor and I’m running out of cash to hire a replacement dual-control vehicle

My livelihood as a self-employed driving instructor is under threat owing to Nissan’s failure to repair my leased dual-control car.

It has been off the road awaiting a spare part for three months, and I’ve now been told it will take at least a further month to arrive.

In order to continue working I have had to hire a dual-control vehicle at a cost of more than £2,500 so far, while also continuing to pay PCP finance of about £1,500 on a car I can’t use.

I have had to borrow more than £1,000 from relatives to extend the hire of the dual-control vehicle. After that, I will have no remaining funds to renew the hire, and will have to stop teaching and lose my customers and my income.

 CW, Eastbourne

You contacted me in mid-March when the latest estimated repair date had been postponed for the third time, until the end of April. Since your hire contract was due for renewal on 15 April, and you had no money left to extend it, time was of the essence.

There was no sense of urgency at Nissan, however. You complained that it had continuously kept you in the dark about timescales and reimbursements, and I had to repeatedly chase it for information.

Meanwhile, you were forking out £490 a month in PCP payments and a monthly hire fee of £952.

I managed to get the company to agree to reimburse you for the hire car costs up to the (as yet unspecified) repair date, but agreeing and paying are different things. Days passed, no money came.

Two weeks after I waded in, Nissan told me the spare part had been sourced and the repair was planned for 15 April, the day your car hire contract ended.

Your reimbursement for the hire, it said, should be paid within 10 days. This meant it would not be with you in time to pay to renew the car hire if the repair was delayed again.

When I pointed this out, the company said it would fund any further hire contracts directly, then refused to put the promise in writing. In the event, your car was repaired in the nick of time.

Next began the battle for compensation. You calculated that, apart from the hire charges, the delays and uncertainty had cost you nearly £900 in lost earnings and other expenses.

Nissan’s response was to offer you two years of free servicing, then it ignored your protest that you had already paid in advance for a service plan and that you were due to replace the car in 12 months.

Back I went to Nissan, and this month it apologised for ignoring you and agreed to pay you compensation, the value of which you have agreed not to disclose.

It says: “We are sympathetic to the customer’s experience, which fell below the high standards Nissan and its dealer partners strive to deliver.”

fullText:
Super-premium Android has top performance, long battery life and good cameras, but is let down by software

Honor’s svelte Android phone-tablet has been given a glow-up for its sixth version, offering a great alternative to Samsung for a fancy foldable with a red suede-like back framed in gold.

The Magic V6 continues the Chinese challenger brand’s strategy of taking a razor-thin device and slapping a giant circular lump on the back to fit in top-class cameras, something others often forgo. It costs a not inconsiderable £1,500 (€1,700/A$2,999) but only until August when the price jumps to a cool £2,000 (€2,300) – a solid £300 more than last year’s model as the cost of RAMageddon continues to bite, even at the very top end of the market.

Other than a new red-backed version, the Magic V6 is almost indistinguishable from the great V5 from last year. It is one of the thinnest and lightest foldable tablets on the market, has a great fingerprint scanner in the power button and has a proper IP68 water resistance rating matching the best slab phones, making it easy to use as a daily driver. When closed it handles just like a regular flagship Android phone with a great, crisp and smooth OLED display.

Once opened, the internal screen is one of the best available, ready for all your media-watching or multitasking needs. But the crease down the middle that allows the screen to fold is slightly more noticeable than some rivals and the integrated screen film is a fingerprint magnet, so it will need cleaning regularly to make the best of it.

Main screen: 7.95in (403ppi) 120Hz OLED flexible display

Cover screen: 6.52in (406ppi) 120Hz OLED

Processor: Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5

Operating system: MagicOS 10 (Android 16)

Camera: 50MP + 50MP ultrawide + 64MP 3x tele; 2x 20MP selfie

Connectivity: 5G, dual sim + esim, USB-C, wifi 7, NFC, Bluetooth 6, GNSS

Water resistance: IP68/69 (1.5 metres for 30 minutes)

Dimensions folded: 156.7 x 74.5 x 8.75-9mm

Dimensions unfolded: 156.7 x 145.6 x 4.0-4.1mm

The Magic V6 has Qualcomm’s top Android chip for 2026, the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5, making it one of the best performers on the market, rivalling top slab phones such as the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra.

However, by default the Magic V6 uses a “balanced” battery mode, which significantly inhibits the phone’s top performance. It isn’t noticeable in day-to-day messaging and browsing but it was in games and other high-intensity tasks. Switching the phone to its “performance” battery mode significantly improved things at the expense of heat and battery life.

The Honor has a very large battery compared with most foldable phone rivals, which helps it last almost two full days between charges while actively using a mixture of the screens for more than eight hours for general browsing, messaging, work and media consumption. Playing games drains the battery a bit faster but the Magic V6 should outlast even the heaviest of usage days.

The phone runs Honor’s version of last year’s Android 16, MagicOS 10, which means it isn’t as up to date as some rivals running Android 17. Honor will provide seven years of Android version and security updates for devices sold within Europe.

MagicOS has improved since last year. It looks quite nice, has plenty of customisation options and tools for making the most of the folding screen, including the excellent ability to split-screen three apps beyond the bounds of the physical display, which was introduced last year.

Various AI tools are strewn throughout the operating system, including Google’s Gemini, which you can set to open in split-screen next to whatever app you are using at the time by quickly flexing the tablet. Many of the tools work as shortcuts for performing tasks such as saving screenshots, editing photos and changing settings on your phone.

The “AI button” is meant to launch actions such as turning on the torch or opening an AI tool by double-tapping, though not depressing, the power button, but it doesn’t work. There are various other parts of the operating system that are unpolished. A bug prevents Google’s Chrome browser from opening in split-screen. Apps that are out of date are described as having a “low version” by Honor’s App Market, which also insists on trying to update apps installed from Google Play, bringing the two app stores into conflict. The Honor lacks the ability to have a different home screen layout for the inside and outside screens, and messaging apps such as WhatsApp routinely insist on opening as small floating windows if you tap a message notification, even on the outside screen.

These little niggles could be overlooked on a significantly cheaper phone, but not on a £1,500-£2,000 device. You can and should expect better.

The enormous circular bump on the back houses three cameras, with a 20MP selfie camera in each of the two screens for a total of five cameras.

The cameras have changed little since last year’s V5 and perform very similarly. The main 50MP camera shoots great photos at 12MP as standard with good detail and range with its cropped 2x zoom, though it can notably suffer from moiré on stripped textures. The 50MP ultra wide camera has been improved since the V5, solving some of the distortion problems. The 64MP 3x telephoto is the best of the bunch, capturing excellent detail, even with its 2x crop zoom for an effective 6x magnification. Its digital zoom remains good to 30x before becoming obviously blown up.

Low light photography is pretty good across all the lenses, while the camera app has tons of features, including many AI tools and a good manual mode for more creative photography. The Magic V6 shoots decent video up to 4K at 60 frames a second and can be used in various partly folded orientations.

The battery will maintain at least 80% capacity after 1,200 full-charge cycles. The phone is generally repairable and Honor publishes pricing for spare parts, including £609 for an internal screen and £152 for the external screen, plus labour and shipping. Honor offers a free screen repair (Care+) for 24 months if bought before 2 August.

The device contains limited recycled materials, which Honor breaks down in the phone’s environmental impact report. The company offers trade-in and refurbished products.

The Honor Magic V6 has an introductory price of £1,499.99 (€1,699.90/A$2,999), which will increase to £1,999.99 (€2,299.90) from August 2026 in some regions.

For comparison, the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra costs £1,899 and the Google Pixel 10 Pro Fold costs £1,749.

The Magic V6 is another very attractive book-style foldable from Honor, but it fails to move things on from last year in an increasingly competitive category.

It has really great battery life, matching some of the best slab phones. The outside screen is great, while the inside screen is good but has a more visible crease than some recent rivals. The Magic V6 feels particularly good when used as a phone, while the massive bump fits in some great cameras and means it doesn’t rock around on a table like some others.

But it is the software that continues to let Honor down. It just isn’t as up to date or polished as it needs to be on a device this expensive.

As good as the Magic V6 is, it lacks a compelling reason to buy it over more complete rivals from Samsung, Google and others.

Pros: slim, light, just like a normal phone when closed, great performance, very long battery life, good internal screen, decent camera, good fingerprint scanner, IP68/9 water and dust resistance rating.

Cons: very expensive, software not as refined as needed, more fragile than a regular device, costly to repair, not much of an upgrade on previous model.

title: Flesh-eating disease could not stop Bowen's dream
description: Ellie Bowen was just 13 months old when her life changed for ever, but she is now set to make her Commonwealth Games debut.
fullText:
Ellie Bowen was just 13 months old when her life changed for ever.

She was diagnosed with necrotising fasciitis, a rare but severe bacterial infection that destroys tissue beneath the skin.

Her parents feared the worst, that they may even lose their baby girl, and while she survived, her right leg was amputated.

Now 17, Bowen is the youngest member of the Welsh athletics squad, is set to make her Commonwealth Games debut.

"Because I had my leg amputated at such a young age, it was just normal to me," she said.

"As I grew older, I think I did see myself as different but then sports made me see further and showed me I can do sport just like anyone else.

"It may look different but the feeling is the same."

Born in Caerphilly, Bowen will realise a childhood dream by representing her country at the Commonwealth Games in the seated shot put.

"I'm really proud of myself. It's been my dream since I was four or five. I said I want to do sports and represent Wales and that's what I'm doing," she said.

Wales at the Commonwealth Games

It was Anthony Hughes, the driving force behind so many of Wales' most successful Para-athletes as performance director at Disability Sport Wales, who first spotted her potential.

He introduced Bowen to wheelchair racing, in which she immediately won medals, before she found a passion for throwing.

"I had just started shot put, discus and javelin when Covid happened. I went back after and was thrown into a competition and I won best performer," she said.

"So I was like, 'oh, I'm OK at it' and then I just kept going and fell in love with it."

It is hard to imagine there will be many spectators at Glasgow's Scotstoun Stadium more proud than Bowen's parents who still regard themselves "lucky" to have her.

"We nearly lost her at 13 months old, but she's here and doing amazing," said her mother Anne.

"Growing up, she wanted to be like her siblings and would say, 'they can ride a bike, why can't I ride a bike?' So she did."

Bowen's determination is only matched by the efforts of her parents to make sure their daughter can achieve her potential in the sport.

Her father Martin built a specially adapted bicycle so she could ride with her family, then moved onto bigger things when he built a campervan to ensure his daughter could to travel to athletics competitions.

"She has just come on so well. Nothing has ever been an obstacle for her," said Martin.

"Whatever you put ahead of her, she'll try and do it and if she can't do it, she'll get around it."

Now Bowen hopes she can make her parents proud when they cheer her on in Glasgow.

"It's the biggest competition I've ever done and I'm just happy to be there," she said.

"It would mean the world to me to win a medal but just being there, I'm so thankful."

title: Police hunt darts match attacker in lobster suit
description: Images are released of a man thought to have attacked another man at the World Darts Championship.
fullText:
Detectives are hunting a man who seriously injured another man, punching and knocking him unconscious following a World Darts Championship match in north London.

The victim, who is in his twenties, was assaulted outside Alexandra Palace on 13 December and is still suffering from "significant injuries" seven months later, police said.

The suspect is believed to have been among a group of men who attended the darts tournament dressed in lobster costumes.

The Met Police has released a CCTV image taken at the venue in the hope of tracing the man and jogging the memory of any witnesses.

The victim was leaving Alexandra Palace at about 16:30 GMT when he encountered the group of men in costume.

He became involved in an argument with them and they were separated by security staff.

Soon afterwards, the victim ran into the group again on the venue's concourse and one of the men punched him, knocking him out.

He later reported the incident to the Met.

Det Con Lizzie Coster, who is leading the investigation, said: "Our thoughts are with the victim in this case, and we hope the best for his recovery.

"This assault occurred outside at a major sporting event, and the suspect was wearing a distinctive costume.

"We are releasing a CCTV image of the suspect in the hope that it will jog the memory of attendees, or anyone else who was in the area at the time."

title: Rogers and Palmer can play together - Alonso
description: Chelsea manager Xabi Alonso says he has a "plan" to play club record £117m signing Morgan Rogers alongside Cole Palmer.
fullText:
Chelsea manager Xabi Alonso says he has a "plan" to play club record £117m signing Morgan Rogers alongside Cole Palmer - and believes the England international will make an "instant impact".

The midfielder became the most expensive British player of all-time when he moved from Aston Villa to Stamford Bridge last week.

The 24-year-old is on holiday after playing for England at the World Cup, while Chelsea have begun their pre-season tour in Sydney.

"In that position we needed an important player and I'm sure there were not many better options than Morgan Rogers," Alonso said.

"You need players who can have that almost instant impact and I'm sure Morgan won't need much time to adapt to the club, the system and his team-mates," Alonso said.

"That was the idea, to get a top player, and Morgan is one of them."

Rogers has signed a six-year contract with Chelsea, with an option for a further year.

Alonso insisted he will be ready, despite not yet taking part in pre-season training, and believes he will be compatible with fellow England international Palmer.

The pair describe each other as being among their "best friends in football", with Rogers saying they would love to play together.

"I have a plan. I have an idea. I can see them linking really well," Alonso said of the pair.

"We need to have a good mix. If we get that balance right and those special players in the right positions, with good control, then we will be more competitive with and without the ball."

Why Rogers and Palmer will thrive together in Alonso's Chelsea

Chelsea in talks for Villa set-piece guru MacPhee

The Blues are also expected to announce the £52m signing of France international defender Maxence Lacroix from Crystal Palace.

The 26-year-old would be Chelsea's oldest signing since 2022.

"We want a squad with the right balance between quality and mentality," Alonso said.

"Those things need to match in terms of maturity, but I think we are starting the new season with good energy. That's important."

Chelsea have also brought in winger Geovany Quenda from Sporting, striker Emmanuel Emegha from Strasbourg and full-back Marco Palestra from Atalanta, and are expected to sign midfielder Valentin Barco, also from Strasbourg, in the coming weeks.

That will leave Chelsea with nearly 40 players in their squad and needing to sell a substantial number of them.

"We need to know that there will probably still be some movement," Alonso added.

"We need to be flexible and quick to act. The main thing is that we have a clear idea, a clear plan that we have built.

"It will probably change before the transfer window closes."

title: REPORT: Browns Exploring Edge Rusher Additions Ahead of Camp
description: After the blockbuster trade of Myles Garrett, Cleveland Browns GM Andrew Berry is hunting for a veteran defensive end to solidify a new-look front before training camp commences.
fullText:
Training camp may be just days away for the Cleveland Browns, but the roster tweaking never stops for Executive Vice President of Football Operations Andrew Berry.

Berry already pulled off a blockbuster trade earlier this summer to send Myles Garrett to the Los Angeles Rams for a handful of picks and on-the-rise edge rusher Jared Verse. He may be looking to bolster the position even more with training camp ramping up.

According to Mary Kay Cabot of Cleveland.com, the Browns are apparently in the market for another edge rusher.

"The Browns are still in the market for a veteran defensive end to add to the rotation and make up for the loss of former Bills edge rusher A.J. Epenesa, who failed his physical," wrote Cabot on Sunday.

She added that Cleveland would prefer to find this mystery edge rusher before training camp commences on Wednesday, but that it may take some time to actually identify someone and sign them.

Cleveland Browns Offseason Report; Which Brown is set for breakout? | Roster rankings fair or foul? The Cleveland Browns are just two weeks away from reporting to camp and then the season will be on for the Browns. Until then, it is another conversation abo...

As Cabot noted, at one point this offseason the Browns were set to sign Buffalo Bills free agent Epenesa to a contract, but balked after being uncomfortable with something that popped up during his physical.

Several months later, the former second-round pick wound up signing a one-year deal with the Philadelphia Eagles instead.

As things stand right now, the Browns boast a pretty strong starting front four along the defensive line, headlined by the newly acquired Verse. The unit also includes veteran DT Maliek Collins, 2025, No. 5 overall pick Mason Graham and 2022 third-round pick Alex Wright.

Behind those four, though, the Browns would benefit from some additional depth for rotational purposes. Cleveland will sorely miss Garrett, for obvious reasons, but building a deeper defensive line that can collectively attempt to make up for what's lost in Garrett's absence could certainly help matters.

Of course, Verse will carry the heaviest burden to replicate as much as he can, Garrett's impact, granted nobody should expect him to be the two-time Defensive Player of the Year.

He won't have to go it alone, though, and another addition to the room will only help ease some of the pressure on him, hence why adding another veteran is of the utmost importance to Berry and company. It sounds like it's just a matter of when, rather than if, Cleveland will be adding another edge rusher to their roster.

title: Corey's time is now and 23XI think they already have a superstar
description: Heim is now in the AJ Foyt, Tim Richmond and Davey Allison territory
fullText:
Heim Time is so incredibly ahead of schedule.

On May 30, 23XI Racing revealed that Corey Heim would finally compete full-time in the NASCAR Cup Series. Since then, all he’s done is look like a legitimate championship contender for a division he isn’t even fully delved into yet.

Over the past five weeks, he’s won twice, at Naval Base North Island and now the Brickyard 400 at Indianapolis Motor Speedway. That doesn’t even include his three Truck Series wins in six starts this season.

The 23-year-old from Marietta, Georgia isn’t an emerging superstar because he already looks like one six months before his inaugural full-time campaign. Bootie Barker, his crew chief, says Heim is simply already one of the best drivers in the division, right now, no argument.

“I think everybody thinks I'm always joking but he's more talented than everybody else,” Barker said. “That’s almost a disservice to some of the great drivers here (but) that's not the case.

"Like all the people we were racing at the end are the best of the best, tremendous. Show much respect to them but Corey is there in talent. Corey is also there in work ethic. He's there as far as a mentality. He has all that now. That's no guarantee going forward, but right now he has it.”

Heim has won twice in eight starts this year, and if it wasn’t for the car not having full-time status, allowing them to qualify even better each week, Barker says they’d have enjoyed even more success.

“If we would have had a better metric in qualifying, we would have won more already,” Barker said.

During the 23XI Racing and Front Row Motorsports v NASCAR antitrust lawsuit, a text message exchange between team owners Denny Hamlin and Michael Jordan was made public, in which the former said they needed to sign Heim to a multiyear deal.

Jordan said ‘lock him up,’ something they successfully executed this past summer. Team president Steve Lauletta said this is early validation.

“Bootie mentioned it, Denny has many times before,” said Lauletta. “That's why Denny has had his eye on him and why Toyota has invested in Corey as much. His approach, his work ethic, his race craft. Just the amount of discipline that he has and maturity that he has just really shows in all of his preparation.

“The relationship he's built with everybody at (the shop) (and) with the other drivers. I just think he's mature beyond his years and it's showing in a very quick way.”

Now, there was a little fortune involved in winning the Brickyard 400 on Sunday, but that is generally the case on Sundays every week. Heim lost the lead when Joey Logano attempted to take him and Denny Hamlin three-wide on the penultimate restart but the three-time champion then pushed him ahead when it mattered the most.

“As we wound down, I was sitting there talking to my spotter Eddie (D’Hondt) and crew chief Bootie,” Heim said. “They both just said, ‘We got to muscle up on this restart’ (and) ‘This is more than likely going to decide the outcome of the race.’

“That was before Denny got the lead on me. Joey tried to put me three there, kill both of our momentum. That got Denny the lead. I thought that was potentially the race. Got another caution. ‘Here we go, might have a shot at it.’ Then Joey gave me a really good push up front.”

And just like that, Heim has won twice in 15 part-time starts, all before his first full-time season. This is something that hasn’t been accomplished since Davey Allison and Tim Richmond won races on a part-time basis in 1987.

Heim is also the first driver to win two of his first 15 starts since AJ Foyt in 1965.

“I'm not much of a stats guy honestly,” Heim said. “Sounds like it's a pretty good one. Definitely cool to be included with a guy like that. Been a crazy year so far. To win two of my first 15 is something I never thought I would accomplish, but here we are. It's a crazy feeling.”

And one of them is a crown jewel that has been won by the likes of Jeff Gordon, Dale Earnhardt, Bill Elliott, Dale Jarrett, Kevin Harvick, Tony Stewart and Jimmie Johnson. Heim is now on that list before he even gets a chance to go points racing next year.

“It's cool to talk about, I guess,” Heim said in his own understated kind of way. “I don't really ever keep up with how many crown jewel wins most guys have, I guess.

“Yeah, I mean, just to be able to win it for myself is just insane. Just super thankful for 23XI, Toyota, everyone that put me in position to do this. Hopefully cross some more off in my career. Who knows, maybe we can win all of them one day. We'll see.”

Again, at this point, he’s ahead of schedule so the sky is the limit.

fullText:
For the second time this month, the Chicago White Sox and Pittsburgh Pirates paired up on a trade.

The Sox acquired right-handed pitcher José Urquidy from the Pirates on Sunday for minor-league pitcher Félix Doroteo.

Urquidy, 31, went 0-1 with an 8.53 ERA and six strikeouts over 6 1/3 innings during five relief appearances for the Pirates from March 29-April 13. He went 5-4 with a 3.66 ERA and 73 strikeouts in 83 2/3 innings in 17 starts with Triple-A Indianapolis.

He was designated for assignment by Pittsburgh on Friday.

Urquidy is 27-17 with a 4.07 ERA and 335 strikeouts in 413 2/3 innings during 86 appearances (70 starts) over seven big-league seasons with the Houston Astros (2019-23), Detroit Tigers (2025) and Pirates (2026).

Doroteo, 21, is 3-2 with a 4.50 ERA and 24 strikeouts in 19 innings over 16 outings (one start) with the Arizona Complex League White Sox this year, his first professional season. He was signed by the Sox as an international free agent on Jan. 15, 2025.

The Sox and Pirates are becoming familiar trade partners. On July 10, the Sox sent infielder Jacob Gonzalez and pitcher Brandon Eisert to Pittsburgh for a Competitive Balance Round A selection (No. 34 overall) in the draft and left-handed pitcher Jaden Woods. The Sox selected Nazareth infielder Landon Thome with the pick the next day.

After Sunday’s trade, the Sox’s 40-man roster increased to 39. The MLB trade deadline is Aug. 3.

He has 53 career NFL starts under his belt and will likely be the team’s QB2 once the three-time Super Bowl champion is back to full strength.

The Chiefs will likely ease Mahomes back before he takes over his QB1 job full-time. Fields will serve as his backup, while Nussmeier and Oladokun will battle for the third-string role.

title: Pirates Problems: Buccaneers Looking for Revenge Against Falcons
description: Haunted by a collapse on "3rd and 28," Tampa Bay targets divisional redemption. New coordinator Zac Robinson and quarterback Baker Mayfield seek personal vengeance against their former employers.
fullText:
The Tampa Bay Buccaneers will likely have to do well in each of their six divisional matchups if they are to finish the season as NFC South champions.

Tampa split each of their series against the Carolina Panthers, Atlanta Falcons and New Orleans Saints last season. Had they won just one more game, the Bucs would have won the division instead of narrowly missing out of the playoffs.

The three divisional losses were by a combined eight points, and the one against Atlanta is probably the most painful.

Any Buccaneers fan is aware of "3rd and 28," as well as coach Todd Bowles' profanity-laced tirade that followed Atlanta's 29-28 win on Thursday Night Football.

Tampa's first chance at revenge against Atlanta will take place Sunday, Nov. 1, at Raymond James Stadium, the scene of the crime. From Atlanta's perspective, the Thursday Night win proved to be a launching pad. The Falcons came into that matchup 4-9, and after beating Tampa, they won their last three games to finish 8-9, tied for the best record in the NFC South.

Although Atlanta lost out on the division championship due to a tiebreaker, the Falcons ended the season flying high. The same can't be said for Tampa Bay, which looked to be a lock to win the South when it was 6-2, but ended up losing seven of its last nine. Things will have to be different in 2026 for Bowles to silence his critics, and they already look different.

Two days after the end of the regular season, Tampa fired offensive coordinator Josh Grizzard after just one season. Tampa replaced Grizzard with the man who engineered "3rd and 28."

The Falcons' late surge wasn't enough to save head coach Raheem Morris' job. When Morris got fired and new head coach Kevin Stefanski came in, Stefanski understandably wanted his guys on staff, including the offensive coordinator.

That made Zac Robinson a free agent, and the Bucs took advantage.

So come November, Robinson will be taking on his former team, and Robinson's quarterback, Baker Mayfield, will be taking on his former head coach.

Stefanski was Cleveland's boss when Mayfield led the Cleveland Browns to their only playoff win since the "new Browns" emerged in 1999.

He was also Cleveland's boss when the Browns made the now-infamous DeShaun Watson trade 14 months later and essentially kicked Mayfield to the curb.

Mayfield hasn't forgotten how things ended in Cleveland, and made it clear that he's no Kevin Stefanski fan.

Beating the Falcons would make a lot of people happy, perhaps Mayfield most of all.
